[4] This Book — Allah sent it down to us as guidance and light. It is not like the rest of the books that are composed; it is not a dry worldly code; it is not a medical book by which diseases and remedies are known; it is not a human history by which events and happenings are known; it is not a volume of belles-lettres by which one is entertained — because all these arts, human power is able to compose their like.

And this Book, which came as guidance and light, lies beyond all of this and gathers all of this together: a constitution for this world and the next, from its descent until the end of time. Every [other] constitution pertains to one country or several countries for a time and is then abrogated, whereas this is a constitution that continues for all generations in all countries. Those before us held fast to this Book — they being the Messenger ﷺ and his Companions — and Allah, Blessed and Exalted, gave them what He had promised them:
Allah has promised those among you who believe and do righteous deeds that He will surely make them successors in the earth, as He made successors those who were before them

and that He will surely establish for them their religion which He has approved for them, and that He will surely exchange their fear for security. They worship Me, associating nothing with Me. And whoever disbelieves after that, those are the transgressors
and it was incumbent upon Us to aid the believers
and to Allah belongs might, and to His Messenger, and to the believers

(Q. 63:8). When the Umma held fast to the Qurʾān, Allah fulfilled these promises for them and they saw it: they took possession of the lands and subdued their people. The strongest states in the world at that time were the Romans and the Persians; the Companions of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ subdued them while they had no machinery, no numbers (

), only sūras of the Qurʾān. Not all of them memorised the whole of the Qurʾān; rather, for each of them it was enough that he have sūras of the Qurʾān — but that he act upon them and hold fast to them. [5] ʿUmar b. al-Khaṭṭāb conquered a quarter of the world and overcame all the states, until he entered Europe and ruled over the people entirely, knowing no arithmetic and no geometry except this Book.

And when the Umma grew heedless of this Book, the Europeans and Yaʾjūj and Maʾjūj, the Easterners, gained mastery over them and overcame them, so they lost the might they had acquired through the Qurʾān. The road of return to might and glory is holding fast to this Book, and holding fast to this Book is not possible for one who does not know its

or its meaning. This is a Book sent down from heaven; Allah, Blessed and Exalted, sent it down upon His Messenger as a bringer of good tidings and a warner. In it He made clear everything He commanded His servants to do, and in it He made clear everything He forbade His servants, and He taught them the happiness He promises them in the hereafter. And whoever does not know this Book, how is he to know to hold fast to it? Coming to understand this Book is indispensable. For this reason the Messenger ﷺ interpreted the Qurʾān, and his Companions [6] interpreted it, and the Umma interpreted it, several

commentaries. This Qurʾān — a promise came down in it at the beginning of its descent, and Allah fulfilled that promise for us with a fulfilment that carries us to a strong hope in everything this Book has promised us. At the beginning of the Qurʾān there came down:
Do not move your tongue with it to hasten it. Its gathering and its recitation are upon Us. So when We have recited it, follow its recitation. Then its clarification is upon Us.

(Q. 75:16–19) This was at the beginning of the descent of the Qurʾān. Allah promised that He would gather the Qurʾān for us, and this Qurʾān was gathered with a gathering for which there is no precedent in any book sent down from heaven or composed on earth. You will not find a house without finding in it a muṣḥaf in which the Qurʾān has been gathered. So
which He promised us — we have seen it as Allah, Blessed and Exalted, promised us.

— He promised us that this Book would of necessity be recited, and this Book has been recited with a recitation for which there is no like in the case of any book. People recited it, the Muslims recited it, the unbelievers recited it, iron recited it, everything recited it. You will not now find a radio station — even in Paris, the enemies of Islam; even in London, the enemies of Islam; even in Israel; even in the seat of His Holiness the Pope — you will not find an Arabic-language station that opens its speech except after a recitation of the Qurʾān. This is as Allah promised us, that this Qurʾān would be recited; it too has been recited with a recitation the like of which has not preceded it for any book.

and the sessions of tafsīr, from the time of the Prophet ﷺ to this day of ours — in a manner for which there is no precedent. [7]

I said that these three promises — Allah has fulfilled for us in them what He promised us, so that our hope has grown strong that everything Allah has promised us in the Qurʾān we shall find as He promised:
We have found what our Lord promised us to be true.

The tafsīr of the Qurʾān is a science, and it is the noblest of the sciences, because the nobility of every science stands in proportion to the nobility of its object. This is the speech of Allah: its relation to our speech is the relation of the Real to creation. So it is the noblest of all the sciences.

Separation is of two kinds: a separation that is being veiled by creation from the Real, Blessed and Exalted — this is a veil; and a separation that is knowing creation through the Real:

[I seek refuge with Allah from Satan the accursed.] The wisdom in beginning the Qurʾān, in opening the recitation with this formula, is that entering upon the King requires knocking at the door and requires asking permission. When the speaker intends to begin reciting the speech of Allah, Blessed and Exalted, he is embarking upon entry into the presence of Allah, Blessed and Exalted, conversing intimately with Him through His speech. For this reason he cleansed [himself] and cleansed his tongue by saying:
So when you recite the Qurʾān, seek refuge with Allah from Satan the accursed.
"Thus Jibrīl taught it to me, from the Tablet, from the Pen, from the Lord, Blessed and Exalted."
This formula is the best of the formulae of seeking refuge. [8]

when he became far off. [9] Iblīs was a servant brought near in the presence of Allah, Blessed and Exalted, as will come in his story tomorrow

I take refuge with Allah from Satan the accursed.

The servant has taken refuge with Allah — [Allah being] a proper name for the Divine Majesty — from Satan, of whom Allah has taught us that he is an enemy to us and whom He has commanded us to take as an enemy. Taking an enemy as an enemy means that you fortify yourself against him and that you take refuge. The servant has nothing but his Lord; he returns to his Lord and takes shelter with Him, taking refuge with Him from the evil of this created thing, which is Iblīs.

A student used to go back and forth to a scholar in Khurāsān until he had memorised from his mouth four thousand items of wisdom. When he took his leave of him to return to his homeland, the scholar said to him: Shall I teach you something better than all the wisdom you have? Is there Iblīs in your country? He said to him: Yes. He said: Does he whisper to you? He said to him: Yes. He said to him: When the enemy of Allah whispers to you, what do you do? He said: We repel him. He said: And if he returns? He said: We repel him. He said: And if he returns yet again? He said: We repel him.
He said to him: You have no power to repel him.
He sees you, he and his tribe, from where you do not see them

(Q. 7:27). But when the enemy of Allah whispers to you, be like the guest: when the householder's dog sets upon him, he seeks protection from the householder; he does not take on the dog himself. When Iblīs whispers to you, take shelter with his Lord; He will suffice you against his evil. Say:
I take refuge with Allah from Satan the accursed.
And I take refuge with Allah from Satan the accursed:

evils fall into classes. There is an evil that attaches to a man's religion — either unbelief, or innovation, or moral dissolution, or a grave sin, or a minor one; all of these are afflictions in a man's religion. Or an affliction in the servant's body: illness, or chronic infirmity, or weakness, or sloth, or cowardice. Or in what belongs to the servant, such as the illness of [his] children, the death

of [his] children, and the loss of wealth — all of these are afflictions. When the servant takes refuge with Allah, he intends by it that he is taking refuge with Allah from all of his evil: an evil that goes back to his religion, an evil that goes back to his body, and an evil that goes back to what he has from Allah, Blessed and Exalted, in the way of blessing. It has been said that the outward form of taking refuge runs counter to gnosis, because fear of what is other than Allah, Blessed and Exalted, is something the gnostics do not accept for themselves, since they see nothing other than Allah, Blessed and Exalted. But this is courtesy towards Allah, Blessed and Exalted, inasmuch as He commanded it. The servant must see his own lowliness and destitution before his Creator. If he wishes, let him play the tyrant over anyone else; but with his Creator he is destitute, weak, incapable of anything — so much so that against the feeble Iblīs he seeks the protection of Allah, Blessed and Exalted, because he is incapable of driving him off. They said: Fear Allah, Blessed and Exalted, because His punishment is severe; and fear the one who fears Allah, because of his supplication; and fear the one who does not fear Allah, because he dreads nothing and refrains from nothing[12]. Taking refuge with Allah, then, is a drawing of strength from Allah and a display of destitution and self-abasement before the Creator, so that He may give him protection from this enemy; and it does not run counter to gnosis, but is rather courtesy towards Allah, Blessed and Exalted. Whoever's station is such that he does not see Satan has no need of taking refuge. Some of the gnostics say: We are a people who do not know Satan. And Allah says:
My servants — you have no authority over them
The Messenger ﷺ was asked about Satan's whispering during the prayer. He said:
[13] For the thief does not enter a house in which there is nothing. The unbelievers and the hypocrites do not experience the whispering

of Satan, because Satan has finished with their case. Everyone who experiences the whispering is truly a believer; it is out of the purity of his faith that he finds the whispering, because the enemy makes war only on one who treats him as an enemy. As for the one who falls in with him, he has finished with him; he has no need of taking refuge.

A human being has a name coined for him together with his coming into existence, and he has names that have supervened upon him, such as owner of the house, owner of the shirt, owner of the book, the scholar, the poet — all of these are names that have supervened upon him. Allah mentioned in the Fātiḥa five of His names, Blessed and Exalted:
al-Ḥamdu li-Llāh (The Praise is for Allah)
is a name. This is the root of the five pillars:
"Islam is built upon five: the testimony that there is no god but Allah"
has the sense of the one who sets right and the one who nurtures, and the servant's prayer nurtures his Islam and sets it right. And
[is] fasting — an intensive form expressing mercy. The servant attained such mercy toward the destitute that he made himself taste the hunger the destitute suffers
so that he might give him alms. This is the pillar of fasting. And
is the pillar of zakāt: he showed mercy to the destitute and so cut off for him a portion of his wealth. And
— this is the ḥajj: just as people are gathered at the place of gathering from every horizon, coming to a single plot of ground, so too is the ḥajj.
At the beginning of the Fātiḥa [the imperative] "Say" is supplied:
al-Ḥamdu li-Llāh (The Praise is for Allah), Lord of the worlds (Q. 1:2)

because the end of the Fātiḥa came down as the speech of the servant. If "Say" is not supplied, the Fātiḥa comes out as though its beginning were the speech of the Lord and its end the speech of the servant; and since we wanted to say that all of it is the speech of the servant, we supplied "Say":
al-Ḥamdu li-Llāh (The Praise is for Allah), Lord of the worlds, The Entirely Merciful, The Especially Merciful, Master of the Day of Judgement … Guide us to the straight path (Q. 1:2–6)
This, of course, is the speech of the servant.

Every praise and every thanks belongs to Allah, Blessed and Exalted, whether [it be for] His attribute or His act. The divisions of praise are four: the Lord's praise of the Lord, the Lord's praise of His servant, the servant's praise of the Lord, and a servant's praise of a servant like himself. All of this belongs to Allah, whether [for] His attribute or His act.
al-Ḥamdu li-Llāh (The Praise is for Allah)
The degrees of the Garden are eight, and
merits the eight ranks of the Gardens. [44]
— the owner of the worlds; a plural of
is everything other than Allah, Blessed and Exalted. It is pluralised in the masculine so as to take in all existent things.
— the bestower of the great blessings and of their outward aspects —
— the bestower of the subtle blessings —
Master of the Day of Judgement (Q. 1:4)

— the King on the Day of Requital. He is the King every day, but every day there is found someone who contests Allah in His dominion in some part of the world; on the Day of Resurrection, however, no one contests Him in His dominion. When He speaks:
To whom belongs the dominion today? (Q. 40:16)
He finds no answer from any human being, so He answers Himself:
To Allah, the One, the Overpowering.
When the servant had praised his Lord with his words:
al-Ḥamdu li-Llāh (The Praise is for Allah), Lord of the worlds, The Entirely Merciful, The Especially Merciful
Master of the Day of Judgement (Q. 1:2–4)
he merited addressing Him, and so he addressed the Presence with his words:
and You alone we ask for help (Q. 1:5)
— we ask help of none but You. When he had praised his Lord, He said to him: put to me whatever you wish of requests. The servant said:
Guide us to the straight path (Q. 1:6)
— he asked guidance of Allah, Blessed and Exalted, to the straight path, and the straight path is the path of the prophets and the messengers. He said:
the path of those upon whom You have bestowed favour (Q. 1:7)
— the prophets: among them are those upon whom Allah bestowed favour.
Or do they envy the people for what Allah has given them of His bounty? For We gave the family of Ibrāhīm the Book and wisdom, and We gave them a great kingship (Q. 4:54)

Among them are those upon whom Allah bestowed favour, so that they combined kingship and prophethood; among them are those whom Allah tried with great trials. Had He said "the path of those who were tried", or "the path of those who were killed", or "the path of those who were slaughtered", the servant would have taken fright at this; but to win the servant over, to rouse him and to set his mind at ease, He said:
the path of those upon whom You have bestowed favour
Not all the prophets were favoured; some of them were tried with the severest trials.
of the prophets, the truthful, the martyrs and the righteous — and good are those as companions (Q. 4:69)
not of those against whom there is anger (Q. 1:7)

— it is related from the Messenger that they are the Jews, and the Qurʾān described them as those with whom He is angry. The Jews are those who knew and did not act upon their knowledge, so Allah became angry with them.
nor of those who go astray (Q. 1:7)

— it is related from the Messenger that they are the Christians. [45] The Christians strayed from the way and did not know it; they did not know the truth, they are merely ignorant, to the point that they made a servant into a lord, out of the depth of their ignorance and their folly. As for the Jews, they knew but did not act upon their knowledge; and the Christians are merely ignorant.
not of those against whom there is anger
nor of those who go astray (Q. 1:7)
is not part of the Qurʾān; it is rather the seal of Allah, Blessed and Exalted, like the seal of the king with which he seals his letters. [46]
By Allah's Name: The Entirely Merciful, The Especially Merciful. Alif Lām Mīm
(Q. 2:1) — Allah knows best what He intends by it.
That is the Book; there is no doubt in it

(Q. 2:2): this Book which Muḥammad ﷺ recites — there is no doubt that it is sent down from Allah, Blessed and Exalted. There is no doubt in this, even if Abū Jahl and his like doubted. They are fools and madmen who have no intellects; their doubt is as though it were no doubt — there is no doubt in it. The sun is the sun even if the blind man does not see it, and honey is honey even if the sick man does not find its taste. So the Qurʾān admits no doubt in it, even if the madmen and the fools doubt it, because it came with proofs and crushing arguments that it is not from any other than Allah, Blessed and Exalted.
(Q. 2:2): a guide for those who travel toward godfearing. This Book — Allah guides by it everyone for whom it was decreed in pre-eternity that he travels toward godfearing.
Those who believe in the unseen
(Q. 2:3): they are those who believe in what is absent from them. The unseen is of two kinds: an unseen that is absent from you — it is the Garden, the Fire, the angels, the

, the resurrection and what lies beyond the resurrection; all of this is absent from you and you have believed in it. And an unseen from which you yourself are absent, O servant, and it is the Presence of Allah, Blessed and Exalted: it is not what is absent — it is present, nearer to you than everything; if you do not find it, then you are the absent one, not it.
And out of what We have provided them they spend (Q. 2:3)
and they spend out of what We have provided them.
And who believe in what has been sent down to you (Q. 2:4)
and what was sent down before you (Q. 2:4)

Belief in what was sent down before the Messenger brings no benefit unless one believes in what was sent down to the Prophet ﷺ. For this reason, whoever believes in all the prophets and disbelieves in the prophet of his own time is an unbeliever. So too with the saints: whoever believes in all the saints and disbelieves in the perfect one of his own age is cut off from Allah, Blessed and Exalted. Belief in what was sent down before you brings no benefit except after belief in what was sent down to you and in what was sent down before you.
and of the hereafter they are certain (Q. 2:4)
they are certain of the hereafter.
who were described with those attributes that we have mentioned.
The guidance we asked for in al-Fātiḥa: these who are described with these attributes have found it.
And it is they who are the successful (Q. 2:5)
those whose triumph is settled, by their deliverance from the Fire and their entry into the Garden made everlasting for them.
He opened the sūra with four

on the hypocrites. Then He called His servants to His oneness, to belief in His Messenger, and to the Garden and the Fire. Then He addressed the Children of Israel through half the sūra. Then He brought the jurisprudence of the religion:
Retaliation is prescribed for you in cases of killing: the free man for the free man
(Q. 2:178). The four descriptions at the beginning of the sūra belong to the four caliphs. The first thing mentioned was
(Q. 2:2), and godfearing is the attribute of Abū Bakr al-Ṣiddīq, may Allah be pleased with him:
And the most godfearing shall be kept far from it, he who gives his wealth to purify himself

(Q. 92:17–18). This was revealed concerning Abū Bakr by agreement. And belief in the unseen is the attribute of ʿUmar b. al-Khaṭṭāb, may Allah the Exalted be pleased with him. On the day ʿUmar embraced Islam, there came down upon the Messenger ﷺ while ʿUmar was embracing Islam:
O Prophet, Allah is sufficient for you, and those of the believers who follow you
(Q. 8:64). Belief is the attribute of ʿUmar.
(Q. 2:3) — this is the attribute of ʿUthmān, may Allah be pleased with him:
Or one who is devoutly obedient through the watches of the night, prostrating and standing, wary of the hereafter
(Q. 39:9). This was revealed concerning ʿUthmān; he used to stand the night in prayer with the Qurʾān.
And out of what We have provided them

this is the attribute of ʿAlī b. Abī Ṭālib, may Allah ennoble his face. He hired himself out in a Jew's garden and kept working until he was paid four dirhams. He gave one dirham in alms before the assembly, one dirham in secret, one dirham by night, and one dirham by day.

Spending is the attribute of ʿAlī, may Allah the Exalted ennoble his face. So everyone who is marked by these attributes is under the banners of these men on the Day of Resurrection. Spending increases the servant's wealth and does not diminish it
"No sun rises but that two angels are at its two sides, one of them saying: O Allah, grant one who spends a replacement, and the other
saying: O Allah, grant one who withholds destruction."

It is related that a servant among Allah's servants asked one of the prophets to supplicate Allah for him that he might find ample provision. So the Prophet ﷺ supplicated Allah, Blessed and Exalted, and Allah answered his supplication. Then he said to him: Inform
my servant, that I have decreed his lifetime [to be] two halves: a half in which he will be poor and a half in which he will be rich. He may choose which of the two I shall begin with for him."

So that prophet ﷺ called the man and informed him. He consulted his wife, and she said: "Tell him: let the ample provision come to you now." The man said to her: "Poverty after wealth is very hard." She said to him: "Do not go against me; just ask for wealth now." So he came to that prophet ﷺ and said to him: "Let wealth come to me now." And wealth came to him. Then the woman said to him: "When you sew a garment for yourself, give a garment as alms to a poor man; and when you buy your food, buy the like of it as alms for a poor man; and when you build a house, make the like of it alms [for] the poor; and when you buy a riding beast, likewise .. everything you do, do the like of it for the poor." So he set about acting on this, and what he had kept increasing, until half his lifetime had passed. Allah revealed to the prophet:
"I had decreed so-and-so's lifetime, half of it
and half of it rich, but I found him grateful, so I have decreed his whole lifetime rich: he will never become poor."
So for this reason spending does not diminish provision. The Messenger ﷺ says:
of the son of Adam there is, each day, an alms."

And the human being has in him, of joints, the number of the days of the year: three hundred and sixty-five parts. Every part of these parts obliges you to bring out an alms for it every day. They said:
"O Messenger of Allah, who is able to do this?"
"Enjoining what is right is an alms; a prayer of two
is an alms; and that you strive with
your brother in his need — whether it is fulfilled or not fulfilled — is an alms."
And bringing gladness [into another's heart]: all of these are alms. Allah completes
through them those alms. O Allah, bless our master Muḥammad and grant him peace.

O Allah, bless our master Muḥammad, the opener of what was closed and the seal of what went before, the helper of the truth by the truth and the guide to Your straight path. We ask Allah, Blessed and Exalted, to grant us and you the understanding of this Book and action in accordance with it, and to complete this work for us as He began it for us, by the standing of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ and to write us down in the register of felicity in this world and the hereafter. O Allah, bless our master Muḥammad and grant him peace.

problems.arabic: ولكن هذه الأسماء كلا إذا تفكرت في معانيها
problems.issue: كلا stands where the syntax requires كلها; a transcription slip rather than a variant.
problems.conjecture: Conjecture: read كلها, translated "all of these names".

problems.issue: The lemma as Niasse cites it matches Q. 16:3 and Q. 39:5 word for word, and he quotes nothing further that would decide between them.
problems.conjecture: Conjecture: reference given as (Q. 39:5); (Q. 16:3) is equally defensible and should be checked against the lesson's other citations.

problems.arabic: كأن شكهم ليس بشك لا شك فيه
problems.issue: The clause is elliptical or damaged: لا شك فيه hangs unattached after ليس بشك.
problems.conjecture: Conjecture: read as two clauses, كأن شكهم ليس بشك، لا شك فيه — translated "their doubt is as though it were no doubt — there is no doubt in it."

problems.issue: لِلْمُتَّفِيرَ is not an Arabic word; the citation is Q. 2:2, glossed at length in ¶69, where it reads لِلْمُتَّقِينَ. The Qurʾānic repair pass appears not to have reached this lemma.
problems.conjecture: Conjecture: read «هُدىً لِلْمُتَّقِينَ» (Q. 2:2), translated "A guidance for the godfearing."

problems.arabic: والتأويل ما يؤيد احتمال الكلام لمعنى به من جهة العقل
problems.issue: The prepositional phrase “li-maʿnā bihi” is syntactically awkward and the referent of the pronoun in “bihi” is unclear; the parallel clause on tafsīr has no corresponding element. Rendered literally as it stands (“admitting of a meaning by it”) rather than emended.
problems.conjecture: CONJECTURE: read لمعنى فيه (“a meaning in it,” i.e. in the speech), the bāʾ/fāʾ confusion being a common OCR substitution; alternatively لمعنى يحتمله.

problems.arabic: ينبغي لكل شارع في فن أن يعرف مبادئه، حدّه
problems.issue: “mabādiʾahu, ḥaddahu” stands as an unlinked apposition with no conjunction, and the list of “principles” breaks off after the first item. The ellipsis is preserved in the English rather than filled out.
problems.conjecture: CONJECTURE: the printed text likely had مبادئه وحدّه, or the passage abridges the standard ten mabādiʾ of a discipline, of which the ḥadd is the first; no emendation made.

problems.arabic: "هل عندكم كتاب خصكم به رسول الله صلى اللٰه عليه وسلم آل البيت؟ قال: لا، إلا
problems.issue: The quotation of the report from ʿAlī is cut by the page break: ¶2 ends on “illā” and the apodosis continues at the head of ¶3. The opening quotation mark in ¶2 is never closed in the transcription. Translated from and to where each paragraph stands; the closing quotation mark is supplied at the end of the continuation in ¶3 and no opening mark is added there.
problems.conjecture: Not a conjecture about wording — a note on the split. The report is the one in Ṣaḥīḥ al-Bukhārī (Kitāb al-ʿilm) with the ṣaḥīfa; nothing is missing between the two paragraphs.

problems.arabic: أعطيه رجل مسلم،.[1] ... فاقبلوا وجوهه"،.[2] ... بالرأي.[3]
problems.issue: Printed page-foot apparatus transcribed into the running text: three footnote reference numerals stand inside the commentary, each preceded by the doubled punctuation “،.” of the transcription. Kept in place as [1], [2], [3]; not moved to an end-note position and not deleted.
problems.conjecture: CONJECTURE: the doubled “،.” is a transcription artefact where the printed text had a single mark before the raised footnote figure; the figures themselves are the edition’s source citations for the two sayings of ʿAlī and for the prohibition of tafsīr bi-l-raʾy.

problems.issue: “uʿṭiyahu rajul muslim”: the verb is unpointed for voice and the noun unmarked for case, so the clause reads either as passive (“granted to a Muslim man”) or as active with “a Muslim man” as subject. Rendered as a passive to match the sense of the report.
problems.conjecture: CONJECTURE: read أُعطِيَهُ رجلٌ مسلمٌ (passive, “which a Muslim man has been given”), as in the standard wording أو فهما أُعطِيَهُ رجل مسلم.

problems.arabic: [4]هذا الكتاب أنزله اللٰه إلينا هدى ونورا
problems.issue: Apparatus in the middle of the commentary: the footnote numeral [4] stands at the very head of the paragraph, before the word it should annotate, where the transcription follows the printed page. Kept where it stands, at the opening of ¶5.
problems.conjecture: CONJECTURE: the figure belongs to the end of the clause that closes ¶4 (“ولابد من نور في قلب المفسر”) and was carried to the top of the next page by the transcription; not moved.

problems.arabic: وراء هذا كلا، وجامعا لهذا كلا
problems.issue: “kullā” written without the final hāʾ or a shadda, twice in this paragraph and once more in ¶7 (“وحكم في الناس كلا”). Either an accusative emphatic كلًّا of the edition’s own orthography or OCR loss of the pronoun. The English (“all of this”; “the people entirely”) is the same on both readings, so no span is marked illegible.
problems.conjecture: CONJECTURE: read كلًّا (adverbial, “entirely”) or كله / كلهم (“all of it” / “all of them”). Preference, on the parallel وجامعا لهذا كلا, is كله in ¶6 and كلهم in ¶7.

problems.arabic: «وَعَدَ اللَّهُ الَّذِينَ آمَنُوا مِنكُمْ ... الَّذِينَ مِن قَبلِهِمْ
problems.issue: The lemma of Q. 24:55 opens in ¶6 with « and is left unclosed at the page break, the remainder standing at the head of ¶7 and closing there with ». The citation is therefore given once, after the last fragment of the run in ¶7, and ¶6 carries no reference.
problems.conjecture: Not a conjecture about wording — a note on the split lemma. No text is missing across the break.

problems.arabic: وليس عندهم آلة ولا عَدد ولا عُدد
problems.issue: The pair ʿadad / ʿudad is distinguished in the transcription only by the vowel on the first consonant, and the second word lacks the shadda that would fix it. Both are kept in the English with the transliteration in parentheses so the distinction is not lost.
problems.conjecture: CONJECTURE: read عَدَد (“numbers”) and عُدَد, for عُدَد plural of عُدّة (“equipment, matériel”) — the standard idiom لا عدد ولا عدد.

problems.arabic: «وَكَانَ حقََّا عَلَيْنَا نَصْرُ الْمُومِنِينَ» — «وَلِلهِ اِڬلْعِزَّةُ وَلِرَسُولِهِڦ وَلِلْمُومِنِينَۖ»
problems.issue: Stacked and duplicated diacritics in the Qurʾānic lemmata (حقََّا with a doubled fatḥa; اِڬل with the small high alif; المومنين spelled without hamza). These are Warsh orthography and pointing artefacts, not damage to the consonantal text, and the words are not in doubt.
problems.conjecture: CONJECTURE: the edition is pointed for the Warsh transmission (المومنين for المؤمنين throughout); the doubled fatḥa on حقا is an OCR duplication of a single حقًا.

problems.arabic: بها.[5] عمر بن الخطاب فتح ربع الدنيا
problems.issue: Footnote numeral [5] transcribed into the running commentary between two sentences. Kept in place.
problems.conjecture: CONJECTURE: the edition’s citation for the preceding statement about the Companions’ holdings of the Qurʾān; no text displaced.

problems.issue: “al-arūbiyyūn” is written defectively, missing the first wāw of الأوروبيون, which ¶7 spells in full (أوروبا). The sense is not in doubt; translated “the Europeans.”
problems.conjecture: CONJECTURE: read الأوروبيون — an OCR or printer’s omission of one wāw.

problems.issue: Apparatus in the middle of a clause: footnote numeral [6] falls between the subject “and his Companions” and its verb “interpreted it,” with a doubled space before it. Kept exactly where it stands rather than moved to the end of the clause.
problems.conjecture: CONJECTURE: the figure annotates فسر القرآن وأصحابه and was set after the word it follows in the printed line; not relocated.

problems.issue: The chunk ends mid-clause on “ʿidda” (“several”), the noun it quantifies falling on the next page. Translated as it stands, with nothing supplied to close the sentence.
problems.conjecture: CONJECTURE: عدة قرون (“for several centuries”) or عدة تفاسير (“in several commentaries”); the continuation is in the following chunk and was not consulted.

problems.arabic: (لَا تُحَرِّكْ بِهِ لِسَانَكَ لِتَعْجَلَ بِهِ ... ثُمَّ إِنَّ عَلَيْنَا بَيَانَهُ»
problems.issue: Unbalanced lemma delimiters: the citation opens with a round bracket and closes with a right guillemet. The chunk otherwise uses « » for Qurʾānic lemmata and round brackets once for a ḥadīth (¶16), so the delimiters are not a reliable guide to register here.
problems.conjecture: Conjecture: a single continuous citation of Q. 75:16–19 running from لا تحرك to بيانه, with no text lost at either edge; treated as one "q" run.

problems.arabic: قرأه الناس، قرأه المسلمون، وقرأه الكفار، وقرأه الحديد، وقرأه كل شيء
problems.issue: وقرأه الحديد is semantically anomalous in a list of reciters (people, Muslims, unbelievers, …, everything). Possible OCR damage. Translated literally as "iron recited it"; nothing silently emended.
problems.conjecture: Conjecture: الحديد is sound and stands for machines — the radio and recording apparatus named in the following sentence about broadcasting stations. Alternative conjecture: OCR corruption of الجديد or الحديث.

problems.arabic: تفاسير، هذا القرآن ... ففسر القرآن أيضا من التفاسير في المؤلفات
problems.issue: The paragraph both opens and closes mid-clause, following the printed pagination: it begins with the bare word تفاسير and breaks off at المؤلفات, whose syntax completes only in ¶10 (ومجالس التفسير …). Translated from where it starts and to where it stops; no beginning or ending supplied.
problems.conjecture: Conjecture: ¶9 opens in the middle of a sentence enumerating the kinds of tafsīr works; the ¶9/¶10 join reads "commentaries among the written works and the sessions of tafsīr … in a manner for which there is no precedent."

problems.issue: Printed footnote marker [7] stands in the running text (as do [8] in ¶16 and [9], [10] in ¶17). Markers retained in place; nothing moved or relocated to a note.
problems.conjecture: Conjecture: the markers key to page-foot apparatus in the printed edition that was not transcribed with the running text in this chunk.

problems.issue: Qurʾānic material carried in straight double quotation marks, which the conventions reserve for ḥadīth or a named authority; and the wording departs from the ʿUthmānic text, which reads قد وجدنا ما وعدنا ربنا حقا (Q. 7:44). Marked "q" because the content is Qurʾān, and cited as "cf."
problems.conjecture: Conjecture: Niasse quoting Q. 7:44 from memory with إنا for قد, or OCR substitution of إنا for قد. Translated as it stands.

problems.issue: Register decision, recorded rather than silently taken: the istiʿādha stands in the lemma delimiters and is the text under commentary, but it is not Qurʾān, and the conventions allow "q" only for actual Qurʾān. Rendered as "i" (transliterated, left untranslated) at every lemma position in ¶15–¶17, with an English gloss supplied in square brackets at its first occurrence.
problems.conjecture: Conjecture: an editor who prefers the formula set as a lemma can retag these "i" runs as "q" wholesale; they are kept as discrete runs so that this is a single mechanical change.

problems.arabic: «فَإِذَا قَرَأْتَ الْقُرْءَانَ فَاسْتَعِذْ بِاللَهِ مِنَ الشَّيْطَنِ الرَّجِيمِ»
problems.issue: Garbled vocalisation and a dropped alif in the Q. 16:98 lemma: بِاللَهِ and الشَّيْطَنِ. No effect on the sense.
problems.conjecture: Conjecture: بِاللَّهِ and الشَّيْطَانِ; translated from the sound reading.

problems.arabic: (هكذا علمنيه جبريل عن اللوح عن القلم عن الرب تبارك وتعالى)
problems.issue: The quoted saying of the Prophet stands in round brackets, the same delimiter used in ¶9 for a Qurʾānic citation. Tagged "h" on the content, not on the bracket type, and set in double quotation marks per the conventions.
problems.conjecture: Conjecture: the printed edition uses round brackets loosely for any quotation; the bracket type carries no register information in this chunk.

problems.issue: التجئ lacks its initial hamza and so cannot be read as the first-person gloss the construction requires.
problems.conjecture: Conjecture: ألتجئ ("I take refuge"), translated accordingly.

problems.issue: The footnote marker falls after the etymological gloss rather than before it, which raises the possibility that the gloss itself is page-foot apparatus transcribed into the middle of the running commentary. Translated where it stands and left in place; not moved into a note and not reordered.
problems.conjecture: Conjecture: either Niasse's own etymology with the marker appended, or a printed note on شطن pulled up into the text at the point where its marker stood. The surrounding clauses read continuously either way, so the question cannot be settled from the transcription alone.

problems.arabic: كما سيأتي في قصته غدا في ، فطُرد ولعن
problems.issue: Material lost after في: a dangling preposition followed directly by a comma. Marked as an illegible span rather than repaired.
problems.conjecture: Conjecture: a reference to where the story of Iblīs is taken up — e.g. في سورة البقرة or في محله ("in its proper place"). One or two words appear to be missing.

problems.issue: The lemma under comment sits inside guillemets, the marking the transcription otherwise uses for Qurʾanic lemmata, but the istiʿādha formula in this first-person form is not Qurʾān (Q. 16:98 has the imperative fa-staʿidh). Marked "p", not "q", per the rule that bracket content is "q" only when it is actually Qurʾān. The same decision is applied at ¶21 and ¶22.
problems.conjecture: Conjecture: the guillemets here mark the text being glossed rather than Qurʾān; if the press prefers lemma-marking over source-marking, these three runs should be re-tagged "q".

problems.issue: OCR damage in the Qurʾānic lemma: يَرَيكُمۡ ("he shows you") for Q. 7:27 يراكم ("he sees you"). Translated from the correct Qurʾānic reading.
problems.conjecture: Conjecture: the ʿUthmānī rasm يرىكم has been read with a dotted yāʾ instead of alif maqṣūra; read يَرَاكُمۡ.

problems.arabic: أنت إذا وسوس لك إبليس التجئ إلى ربه
problems.issue: Pronoun suspect: ربه ("his Lord") where the second person ربك ("your Lord") would be expected after التجئ. Translated as it stands ("his Lord"), which the dog-and-householder simile actually supports: the guest appeals to the dog's own master.
problems.conjecture: Conjecture: either ربك mis-set as ربه, or deliberate — Iblīs's own Lord, matching يستجير برب المنزل earlier in the sentence. Retained the latter reading.

problems.issue: Printed page-foot apparatus transcribed into the running commentary: the footnote numeral [11] stands at the head of the paragraph, before the lemma. Kept where it stands, not moved.
problems.conjecture: Conjecture: a page-break footnote reference from the printed edition; its note text was not transcribed.

problems.issue: The paragraph ends mid-construct (موت, "the death"), the printed page having broken there; ¶23 opens with its genitive (الأولاد). The English is left equally incomplete at both ends rather than completed.
problems.conjecture: Conjecture: the continuous clause is موت الأولاد, "the death of [his] children".

problems.issue: Printed page-foot apparatus transcribed into the middle of the running commentary: the footnote numeral [12] falls inside the quoted maxim, before إذاً الإستعاذة. Kept in place.
problems.conjecture: Conjecture: footnote reference for the source of the three-fold خف maxim; note text not transcribed.

problems.issue: The lemma is opened with « but never closed, and the paragraph stops at a full stop inside the citation. The quoted words are shared verbatim by Q. 15:42 and Q. 17:65, so the reference cannot be fixed from the lemma alone; cited as (Q. 15:42).
problems.conjecture: Conjecture: Q. 15:42 (the continuation إلا من اتبعك من الغاوين suits the argument about those over whom Satan has no power), but Q. 17:65 is equally possible and the closing guillemet is lost.

problems.issue: Two things: the parenthesis encloses ḥadīth, not Qurʾān, so it is tagged "h"; and the footnote numeral [13] from the printed page foot stands immediately after it, inside the running commentary. Numeral kept where it stands. The transcription reads تلك where the canonical wording has ذاك/ذلك.
problems.conjecture: Conjecture: ذاك محض الإيمان (Muslim); the demonstrative may have been normalised by the transcriber rather than damaged. Translated as transmitted here.

problems.issue: The paragraph ends mid-construct (وسوسة, "the whispering"), with its genitive (الشيطان) opening ¶25. Both halves are translated as they stand.
problems.conjecture: Conjecture: the continuous clause is وسوسة الشيطان, "the whispering of Satan".

problems.arabic: خرج الرسول صلى اللٰه عليه وسلم يوما إلى المسجد
problems.issue: Register decision, not damage: ¶26–¶27 report a prophetic encounter, but the Arabic carries no brackets or quotation marking anywhere in it and the dialogue is embedded in Niasse's own narration. Tagged "p" throughout, on the pattern of the Khurāsān story at ¶19, rather than "h".
problems.conjecture: Conjecture: if the press wants prophetic speech set off wherever it occurs, the قال turns of the Prophet in ¶26–¶27 would need re-tagging as "h"; the Arabic gives no warrant for doing so.

problems.arabic: أُجعل في قدر محموم حتى لا أمنعهم من الصدقة.[14]
problems.issue: The clause is logically inverted: asked why he keeps the community from almsgiving, Iblīs answers that he is put in a cauldron "so that I do not keep them from almsgiving" (حتى لا أمنعهم), which reverses the sense the other three answers establish. Translated as it stands. The footnote numeral [14] from the printed page foot follows it inside the running commentary and is kept there.
problems.conjecture: Conjecture: the negative لا is intrusive — read حتى لا أقدر أن أمنعهم ("so that I am unable to keep them") or simply حين أمنعهم ("when I keep them"); compare أبقى محموما at ¶26.

problems.issue: Register decision, not damage: the "i" tag is applied to transliterated common nouns left untranslated — jihād (¶27, twice) and salām (¶26). Proper names (Iblīs, Khurāsān, Ramaḍān) and the fixed renderings (Allah ﷺ) are left inside the "p" runs, since the conventions govern those under transliteration and fixed renderings rather than under "i".
problems.conjecture: Conjecture: if the press italicises month names and other transliterated proper nouns as well, Ramaḍān and Khurāsān would need splitting out as "i" too.

problems.issue: The chunk ends here, mid-episode and without terminal punctuation in the Arabic; Iblīs is left tied to the pillar and the outcome falls in the next chunk. No ending supplied.
problems.conjecture: Conjecture: the sentence continues into ¶28 (chunk L01-04).

problems.issue: The transcribed form does not match the Ḥafṣ/Warsh rasm of Q. 11:41, which reads مَجْرَاهَا وَمُرْسَاهَا (verbal nouns, 'its course and its mooring'). The forms here are active participles. Not silently normalised.
problems.conjecture: CONJECTURE: a transcription of the variant qirāʾa مُجْرِيهَا وَمُرْسِيهَا, with Allah as the referent of the participles; translated accordingly as 'the One who makes it sail and the One who brings it to anchor'. OCR corruption of مجراها ومرساها cannot be excluded. If the verbal-noun reading is adopted, render 'By Allah's Name is its course and its mooring.'

problems.issue: The lemma is cited as a bare imperative without its conjunction, so the āya cannot be fixed with certainty.
problems.conjecture: CONJECTURE: Q. 7:158 (وَاتَّبِعُوهُ), which commands following the Prophet and so fits the argument; the reference given in the output. Q. 6:153 (فَاتَّبِعُوهُ, of the path) and Q. 6:155 are the alternatives.

problems.issue: The sentence is split across the ¶35/¶36 boundary by the printed pagination: ¶35 ends at إلى and ¶36 opens with الأبد. Each paragraph is translated from where it starts; nothing is supplied to close ¶35 or to open ¶36, and the halves are not joined.
problems.conjecture: CONJECTURE: من الأزل إلى الأبد, 'from pre-eternity to everlasting end'. The same mid-sentence split occurs at ¶29/¶30 (وعلى رأسهم الشافعي / من قال) and ¶32/¶33 (ونحن واجب / علينا), and ¶28 opens mid-narrative.

problems.issue: OCR vocalization damage: a kasra stands on the waṣl alif of the article (اِلرَّحْمَنِ). The reading is not in doubt, so no illegible span is marked.
problems.conjecture: Conjecture: read ٱلرَّحْمَٰنِ ٱلرَّحِيمِ. The same fault recurs in ¶41 as إِلرَّحِيمِ (hamza for waṣl alif).

problems.arabic: وقيل من أله إذا عبد، الإله
problems.issue: The paragraph ends mid-clause because the printed edition breaks the page here; ¶38 resumes with المعبود. Translated from where it starts and stops; no beginning or ending supplied beyond the bracketed copula [is].
problems.conjecture: Conjecture: the continuous clause is الإله المعبود, 'the ilāh is the one worshipped.'

problems.arabic: وهو في نفسه صفته الرحمة "كتب على نفسه الرحمة"
problems.issue: The first occurrence of this Qurʾānic phrase is set in double quotation marks, i.e. in the transcription's ḥadīth punctuation, while the second occurrence later in the same paragraph is set in Qurʾānic guillemets. Both are marked "q" because both are Qurʾān.
problems.conjecture: Conjecture: Q. 6:12; the same wording also stands at Q. 6:54, and Niasse does not specify which.

problems.arabic: أنعم فقط وليس خطأً، إنما هو هذه صفته
problems.issue: Elliptical oral phrasing, further obscured by the unexpected accusative خطأً. Rendered literally ('He bestowed favour outright, and not by mistake; rather this is His attribute') with nothing supplied.
problems.conjecture: Conjecture: the sense is that His bestowal of mercy follows from His essential attribute, not from any lapse or accident.

problems.issue: OCR damage to the lemma's final word: عَشَرٌّ carries both tanwīn and shadda, neither of which belongs to the indeclinable numeral.
problems.conjecture: Conjecture: read عَلَيْهَا تِسْعَةَ عَشَرَ (Q. 74:30).

problems.arabic: قام كل حرف بينه وبين واحد من الزبانية لا يدخله النار أبدا
problems.issue: The clause is grammatically unstable as transcribed: النار stands in the nominative after a transitive-looking لا يدخله, which would yield 'the Fire never enters him.' Rendered as 'so that he never enters the Fire' and flagged rather than emended.
problems.conjecture: Conjecture: read لا يُدخِلُهُ النارَ أبدا, 'it [the angel] never casts him into the Fire,' or else لا يَدخُلُ النارَ أبدا, 'he never enters the Fire.'

problems.arabic: ففتشوا فيها فوجدوا (بِسْمِ اللَّهِ الرَّحْمَن الرَّحِيم.[28]
problems.issue: The opening parenthesis of the final lemma is never closed, the last two words lose their case endings, and the footnote marker [28] stands where the closing bracket should be. The lemma boundary is therefore editorial.
problems.conjecture: Conjecture: the lemma ends at الرَّحِيمِ and the closing parenthesis dropped out before the footnote marker; read (بِسْمِ اللَّهِ الرَّحْمَٰنِ الرَّحِيمِ).

problems.issue: Page-foot apparatus markers from the printed edition are transcribed into the running commentary at ¶38 (twice), ¶40, ¶41 (twice) and ¶42. Each is retained at exactly the point where the transcription places it; none has been moved, and no footnote text accompanies them in this chunk.
problems.conjecture: Conjecture: the markers key source-references for the ḥadīth and grammatical positions cited; the notes themselves fall outside this chunk.

problems.issue: ¶43 and ¶44 are printed sūra-heading matter (title, then the provenance-and-count line), transcribed as free-standing paragraphs in the middle of the running commentary. Translated where they stand and left in place.
problems.conjecture: Conjecture: in the printed edition these are the sūra head and its subhead, not spoken text; 'Meccan — seven āyāt.'

problems.issue: A sūra rubric ("Meccan; seven āyas") stands at the end of the running commentary, where the printed edition's heading/page apparatus has been transcribed into the body of the text. Translated where it stands and not moved; its rubric character is marked in square brackets.
problems.conjecture: Conjecture: the printed heading مكية، سبع آيات, belonging above the sūra and not to Niasse's spoken sentence.

problems.issue: Footnote reference markers [29]–[42] from the printed page-foot apparatus are transcribed into the running text, some of them mid-clause (e.g. [29] in ¶45, [31] in ¶46, [35] in ¶48) and one at the head of a paragraph ([39] at the start of ¶53). All are retained in place and none has been moved; the apparatus notes themselves are not present in this chunk.
problems.conjecture: Conjecture: the markers are the transcriber's retention of the edition's footnote numbering, not Niasse's words.

problems.issue: OCR damage in the Qurʾānic lemma: final yāʾ appears as the Warsh-orthography glyph ے, and the word carries stray vowel/hamzat-waṣl marks (اَ۬ل).
problems.conjecture: Conjecture: المثاني (Q. 15:87), the reading being secure; translated as such.

problems.arabic: أنزلت علي كانت كنزا تحت العرش
problems.issue: The ḥadīth text is syntactically broken: two finite verbs are juxtaposed with no connective, so the span is not construable as transcribed. Translated as it stands, asyndetically.
problems.conjecture: Conjecture, not an emendation: either أُنزلت عليَّ وكانت كنزاً تحت العرش ("it was sent down to me, and it had been a treasure beneath the Throne") or, matching the better-known wording, أُنزلت عليَّ من كنز تحت العرش ("it was sent down to me from a treasure beneath the Throne").

problems.arabic: لأنها ورد أن فاتحة الكتاب شفاء
problems.issue: Gender/number agreement broken: the feminine pronoun -hā on لأن has no predicate, since ورد أن follows with its own clause. Rendered impersonally ("because it has been transmitted that").
problems.conjecture: Conjecture: لأنه ورد أن (impersonal), or لأنها شفاء، ورد أن.

problems.arabic: الحسن بن علي كرم اللّٰه وجهه
problems.issue: The eulogy كرم اللّٰه وجهه, conventionally attached to ʿAlī, here follows al-Ḥasan b. ʿAlī. Translated where it stands ("may Allah ennoble his face") without reassignment.
problems.conjecture: Conjecture: the printed text had the eulogy on علي (i.e. الحسن بن علي كرم اللّٰه وجهه referring to the father), or رضي اللّٰه عنه for al-Ḥasan; the transcription preserves the ambiguity.

problems.issue: OCR damage: hamza lost from the medial position.
problems.conjecture: Conjecture: تُؤذِن بالفراق ("gives notice of separation"); translated as such.

problems.arabic: فأتوا إلى الضيف قالوا لهم ... ولكن طلبناكم العشاء ولم تعطونا
problems.issue: Oral-register and non-classical forms retained, not emended: singular الضيف with the plural pronoun لهم; طلبناكم العشاء with a double accusative in place of طلبنا منكم; and ولم تعطونا with the indicative for the expected jussive تُعطونا > تعطوا.
problems.conjecture: Conjecture: these are features of the transcribed oral delivery rather than OCR error; translated literally.

problems.issue: OCR damage in the proper name: yāʾ misread as a hamza-bearing tooth.
problems.conjecture: Conjecture: شيث بن آدم, i.e. Shīth (Seth) son of Ādam; translated as such. The arithmetic confirms the list (50 + 30 + 10 + 10 + 4 = 104).

problems.issue: Two names stand in bare apposition with no connective; the identification is supplied in square brackets.
problems.conjecture: Conjecture: إدريس وهو أخنوخ ("Idrīs, who is Akhnūkh/Enoch").

problems.arabic: والفرقان كل اجتمع في فاتحة الكتاب
problems.issue: كل stands without its pronominal suffix, leaving the subject incomplete; the missing element is supplied in square brackets.
problems.conjecture: Conjecture: والفرقان كله اجتمع في فاتحة الكتاب ("and the Furqān, all of it, is gathered in Fātiḥat al-Kitāb").

problems.issue: OCR damage in the vocalisation of the lemmata: ألرَّحْمَنِ carries a hamza on the article in place of hamzat al-waṣl, and the alif of الرَّحْمَٰنِ is unwritten. مَلِكِ is left as transcribed (Warsh reading) and not assimilated to مَالِكِ.
problems.conjecture: Conjecture: الرَّحْمَٰنِ الرَّحِيمِ (Q. 1:3); مَلِكِ يَوْمِ الدِّينِ (Q. 1:4) is the Warsh reading and is translated accordingly as "King of the Day of Judgement".

problems.issue: OCR damage: the final verb carries a tanwīn (-un) impossible on an imperfect verb.
problems.conjecture: Conjecture: وَإِيَّاكَ نَسْتَعِينُ (Q. 1:5); translated as such.

problems.issue: OCR damage: hamzat al-waṣl written as hamzat al-qaṭʿ (إهْدِنَا), and defective alif in الصِّرَطَ.
problems.conjecture: Conjecture: اهْدِنَا الصِّرَاطَ الْمُسْتَقِيمَ (Q. 1:6); translated as such. The same defective spelling recurs in ¶57 (صِرَطَ ألذِينَ, for صِرَاطَ الَّذِينَ).

problems.issue: OCR damage: tāʾ marbūṭa written as hāʾ.
problems.conjecture: Conjecture: موعظة ("admonition"); translated as such.

problems.issue: The paragraph opens mid-sentence, completing the list of genres begun in ¶57; it is translated from where it starts, with no beginning supplied.
problems.conjecture: Conjecture: continues ¶57's موعظة وتذكير ("admonition and reminding"), the ninth of the nine funūn announced in ¶54. ¶47–¶51 break mid-clause in the same way, at وتسمى | الراقية, إلا السام، والسام | الموت, and فإذا فاتحة | الكتاب, and are likewise left as they stand.

problems.arabic: (بني الإسلام على خمس شهادة أن لا إله إلا الله)[43] ... (وإقام الصلاة)
problems.issue: The transcription puts a ḥadīth inside the round brackets that the edition elsewhere reserves for Qurʾānic lemmata, and the ḥadīth is broken in two by Niasse's gloss of lā ilāha illā Llāh, with the second half left as a bare bracketed fragment at the end of the paragraph. Marked "h" in both places, not "q".
problems.conjecture: Conjecture: the printed edition set the ḥadīth (Bukhārī/Muslim, bunī al-islām ʿalā khams) in the same brackets as the lemmata; the enumeration continues past (وإقام الصلاة) in the following paragraphs, which here open mid-list.

problems.issue: Unvocalised, so the reading Malik or Mālik cannot be determined from the transcription; the same phrase is مَالِكِ in ¶64 and ملِكٍ in ¶65. Rendered uniformly "Master of the Day of Judgement".
problems.conjecture: Conjecture: مَالِكِ يَوْمِ الدِّينِ throughout, following ¶64, which is the only fully pointed occurrence.

problems.issue: Footnote reference number carried into the running commentary by the transcription; no accompanying note text appears anywhere in this chunk. Left in place, unmoved, as [43]. The same applies to [44] in ¶64, [45] in ¶66 and [46] in ¶67.
problems.conjecture: Conjecture: the four markers belong to page-foot apparatus of the printed edition that was not transcribed; they are reference numbers only, not apparatus content.

problems.arabic: والرحمن صيام صيغة مبالغة في الرحمة
problems.issue: صيام stands with no copula or particle between الرحمن and صيغة مبالغة, which breaks the pattern of the surrounding list (al-Rabb → prayer, al-Raḥīm → zakāt in ¶61, Mālik yawm al-dīn → ḥajj in ¶61). Translated as it stands with the copula supplied in brackets.
problems.conjecture: Conjecture: والرحمن الصيام، صيغة مبالغة في الرحمة — "and al-Raḥmān is fasting; [it is] an intensive form expressing mercy". A word may have dropped out after الرحمن.

problems.arabic: ولما أحيبنا أن نقول كلها من كلام العبد
problems.issue: أحيبنا is not an Arabic word; ب and ي have been exchanged by the OCR. Translated from the conjecture.
problems.conjecture: Conjecture: أحببنا — "since we wanted / preferred".

problems.issue: الْمُسْتَفِيمَ for الْمُسْتَقِيمَ — qāf read as fāʾ (dot count). The same error recurs in the lemma opening ¶66 (الْمُسْتَفِيمَ), while the unbracketed repetitions in ¶66 are correctly spelled المستقيم. Also إهْدِنَا is set with hamzat qaṭʿ for hamzat waṣl. Translated from the conjecture.
problems.conjecture: Conjecture: اِهْدِنَا الصِّرَاطَ الْمُسْتَقِيمَ.

problems.issue: Vowel signs scrambled and the final two consonants transposed: ـيَن for ـينَ, and the alif of الْعَالَمِينَ is absent. The same word is اِلْعَلَمِينَ at the end of ¶64 and الْعَلَمِينَ in ¶64, the hamzat waṣl sign having been mis-set over the article.
problems.conjecture: Conjecture: رَبِّ الْعَالَمِينَ in all three places.

problems.issue: The lemma الرَّحِيمِ carries a closing round bracket with no opening bracket, so the boundary between the preceding gloss (وظواهرها) and the lemma has to be restored from sense. Marked "q" for الرحيم and "p" for the glosses on either side.
problems.conjecture: Conjecture: (الرَّحِيمِ) المنعم بدقائق النعم.

problems.issue: Both fragments of Q. 40:16 are misvocalised: الْيَوْمُ for الْيَوْمَ (the adverbial accusative), لِلِهِ for لِلَّهِ, and اِلْقَهّارِ with hamzat waṣl mis-set and the shadda misplaced for الْقَهَّارِ. Translated from the Qurʾānic text.
problems.conjecture: Conjecture: «لِمَنِ الْمُلْكُ الْيَوْمَ» ... «لِلَّهِ الْوَاحِدِ الْقَهَّارِ».

problems.issue: Kasra with tanwīn on the first term of a construct phrase is impossible, and the alif of مالك is absent; the lemma also opens with no opening bracket because the run began at the end of ¶64. Translated as the continuation of that run, not as a new lemma.
problems.conjecture: Conjecture: مَالِكِ يَوْمِ الدِّينِ, as pointed in ¶64.

problems.arabic: قال له اقترح على كل ما شئت من المطالب
problems.issue: اقترح على is unintelligible without a pronoun; the yāʾ of the first-person pronoun has dropped. Translated from the conjecture.
problems.conjecture: Conjecture: اقترح عليَّ كل ما شئت من المطالب — "put to me whatever you wish of requests".

problems.issue: وَايَّاكَ for وَإِيَّاكَ (hamza lost) and نَسْتَعِينَ for نَسْتَعِينُ (indicative, not subjunctive). Translated from the Qurʾānic text.
problems.conjecture: Conjecture: (وَإِيَّاكَ نَسْتَعِينُ).

problems.issue: صرْط for صِرَاطَ (alif absent, sukūn on the rāʾ) and ألذِينَ for الَّذِينَ (hamza for the article, shadda absent). Translated from the Qurʾānic text.
problems.conjecture: Conjecture: (صِرَاطَ الَّذِينَ أَنْعَمْتَ عَلَيْهِمْ).

problems.arabic: «اَمْ يَحْسُدُونَ اَ۬لنَّاسَ ... وَءَاتَيْنَٰهُم مُّلْكاً عَظِيماࣰۖ» ... «مِّنَ اَ۬لنَّبِيٓـِٕۧنَ ... وَحَسُنَ أُوْلَٰٓئِكَ رَفِيقاࣰۖ»
problems.issue: These two citations (Q. 4:54 and Q. 4:69) are transcribed in Warsh orthography and vocalisation (اَ۬ for the article with hamzat waṣl, فَقَدَ اٰتَيْنَآ for فَقَدْ آتَيْنَا), unlike the Fātiḥa lemmata around them, which are in Ḥafṣ-style pointing. Not an OCR defect, but the mixture should be regularised by the press at proof.
problems.conjecture: Conjecture: the transcription drew these two verses from a Warsh text or font while the lemmata came from the printed edition; no emendation made.

problems.issue: ألضَّالِينَ for الضَّالِّينَ — hamza for the article and the shadda on the lām lost; the lemma also opens with no opening bracket because the run began at the end of ¶66. Translated as the continuation of that run.
problems.conjecture: Conjecture: (وَلَا الضَّالِّينَ). The same spelling defect stands at وَلَا الضَّالِينَ in ¶66.

problems.arabic: سورة البقرة / مائتان وست وثمانون آية
problems.issue: ¶68 and ¶69 are the printed edition's sura head and verse count, transcribed as two separate paragraphs of running text in the middle of the commentary stream. Translated where they stand and kept as separate paragraphs; not moved and not merged.

runs: Allah is not ashamed to strike a parable of whatever kind — a gnat, or what is above it
This āya was revealed in reply to what the Jews said when Allah struck the parable of the fly in His saying, Exalted:
And if the fly should snatch anything from them, they could not recover it from it
and in [the case of] the spider, in His saying:
like the likeness of the spider

They said: What did Allah intend by mentioning these contemptible things? It is not fitting that Allah, Blessed and Exalted, should strike a parable with these paltry things; He ought to have been ashamed of that. And so it was revealed. This is the occasion of the revelation of this āya. Allah struck the parable with these paltry things, and the disbelievers and the hypocrites and the Jews objected to striking a parable with the like of these with respect to the Majestic One, Blessed and Exalted
So Allah replied to them with His saying:
Allah is not ashamed to strike
a parable of whatever kind — a gnat, or what is above it
Allah is not ashamed to take the gnat as a likeness, or what is below it, or what is above it; He does not omit to make plain the wisdom it contains.
But as for those who believe, they know that it
[that is,] the firmly established, falling in its proper place
When He strikes a parable with these things, people fall into two classes: the believers know that the parable falls in its proper place.
And as for those who disbelieve, they say: What did Allah intend by this as a parable
from the truth, because of their disbelief
and He guides by it many
of the believers, because of their holding it true
and He leads none astray by it except the transgressors
He is not ashamed to strike a parable.

— shame — is the servant's shrinking back when he does something for which he would be reproached or blamed, so that he leaves it off. Shrinking back out of aversion to what one is blamed for: this is impossible with respect to Allah, Blessed and Exalted. We have told you a rule: every attribute that is impossible of Allah, Blessed and Exalted — if you look closely into it you find that it has a beginning and an end; its beginning is impossible with respect to Allah, Blessed and Exalted, and its end is admissible with respect to Him.

is the shrinking back from something for which one is blamed or reproached, so that he leaves it; his leaving it is the end. As for the leaving, it is admissible of Allah, Blessed and Exalted. And since nothing keeps the great man from doing a thing except shame — for he fears no one, so nothing restrains him except shame — and Allah, Blessed and Exalted, is greater than every great one, shame is predicated of Him without qualification while what is meant is the leaving: that He does not leave it off out of shame. As for the disbelievers who faulted the striking of a parable with these paltry things, [they did so] out of their dullness and the blindness of their hearts, for these paltry things are the most remarkable of what Allah, Blessed and Exalted, created, and they hold wonders that nothing else holds. The gnat, for example, for all the smallness of its frame, has in it every organ that is in the elephant, and two wings besides. Allah, Blessed and Exalted, who had the power to create the elephant and to create the gnat and to fit into it as many organs and joints as are in the elephant — nothing defeats Him. And this creature, which is the small gnat: when Allah created it weak, and created the fly weak likewise, He put in it such boldness that it holds no one in awe. When people gather you find the fly hovering over their eyelids and over their eyes; however hard they drive it off it comes back at them, caring nothing for them. Even kings, even tyrants — the gnat alights on them and does not fear them. As for the elephant and the lion, Allah created them at the utmost of strength and solidity that they could be, and He fitted cowardice into them, so that they do not dare to come near people; they dwell in

the wastelands, and when the two of them hear the sound of a human being they both flee from him. This belongs to the kindness of Allah, Blessed and Exalted. This boldness and audacity which is in lowly things — had He placed it in these powerful things, they would have harmed people, rather would have destroyed them in a short span. If the lion acted as audaciously toward a human being as the fly and the mosquito act audaciously toward him, the people would [all] die. But out of His kindness, Blessed and Exalted, He placed fear in the strong and placed boldness in the weak, which harms no one. The fly, when it alights on you, embitters your life for you; you are in your house, or in your garden, or in whatever place — it embitters your life for you. And the mosquito likewise, for all the lowliness of these things, their weakness and their incapacity. So how do you act boldly toward Allah, Blessed and Exalted, given the severity of His punishment and what is in Hell of scorpions and snakes whose injury never ceases? Everyone who contravenes the command of Allah, Blessed and Exalted, and abandons what Allah has commanded him, is as though he were acting audaciously toward this severe punishment — while a flea or a mosquito or a fly embitters him and clouds his life for him. Let him know that he can endure nothing of the punishment of Allah, Blessed and Exalted. And these things, for all their lowliness, did not prevent the parable from falling exactly in its place:
O people, a parable has been struck, so listen to it. Those whom you call upon apart from Allah will never create a fly
This is brilliance of the highest order. And He struck a parable for the worship of idols:
Their likeness is as the likeness of the spider: it took a house; and the frailest of houses is the spider's house
And the striking of parables by means of such things occurs in the Books sent down before the Qurʾān.

al-Maʾmūn was on his pulpit when the fly alighted on him. He drove it off, and it alighted on him repeatedly, and he drove it off, and he had no power over it in anything. So he sent to Abū Hudhayl, a scholar in the city, asking him: what is the wisdom in Allah's creating these things?

"Allah created these things as a humiliation for tyrants of your sort. For when the tyrant king sits upon his throne, the fly alights on his excrement and then alights on him, and he is unable to drive it away."
"You have spoken truly. For this Allah created it, Blessed

and Exalted.[2] They have said: were it not for the winds and the flies, the world would stink.[3] Along with that, these foul odours — the flies eat them and the winds carry them off, so they dissipate. Were it not for that, the world would stink and it would harm its inhabitants. He said
He leads many astray by it and He guides many by it

(Q. 2:26). How did He, Great is His Majesty, say that He guides many, when the people of guidance are the few in relation to the people of error? The people of error are many, and the people of guidance are few; yet despite their fewness they are many in themselves — not in relation to the people of error, but in themselves they are many. Or: the people of truth, even if they are few, are the great mass, and they are the many, and they are the ones who prevail, and it is they who count. But in reality those who stray are more numerous than those who are guided, and that is because faith is precious and because Allah, Blessed and Exalted, has no need [of anyone]. Had He willed, everyone on earth would have believed, all of them together:
And had your Lord willed, everyone on earth would have believed, all of them together
(Q. 10:99). But because He has no need of creation, He made most of the jinn and of humankind people of error.
And He leads none astray by it except the transgressors
those who go outside His obedience.
(Q. 2:27): what He enjoined upon them in the scriptures, namely faith in Muḥammad ﷺ. Allah's covenant is of three kinds. The first is what He took upon the progeny of Adam on the day of
Am I not your Lord? They said: Yes
(Q. 7:172). The second is what He took upon the messengers: that if they lived to meet the Prophet ﷺ, they would believe in him and follow him. The third is what He took upon the scholars:
You shall surely make it clear to the people and not conceal it

(Q. 3:187). This covenant the Jews broke. He made the covenant something broken, as though He had made it a rope, because in the speech of the Arabs a covenant is called a rope; for this reason the expression "breaking" is admissible.
and they sever what Allah has commanded to be joined
: faith in the Prophet, the ties of kinship, and other than that.
and they work corruption in the earth
: by acts of disobedience and by hindering [people] from faith.
(Q. 2:27): because their destination is the Fire made everlasting for them.
(Q. 2:28): drops of seed in the loins
in the wombs, in this world, by the breathing of the spirit into you. And the interrogative expresses astonishment: how do they disbelieve after [all] this?
then He causes you to die
at the expiry of your appointed terms.
(Q. 2:28): you will be brought back after the resurrection, and He will requite you for your deeds. And He said, as a proof of the resurrection when they denied it:
He it is who created for you what is in the earth

He cast a specious argument upon the angels. Had Allah not refuted it, we could not have refuted it; no one can refute it by reason. He said: I know that Allah is my Lord and my Creator and my Owner. Why did He create me, after He knew that I am damned [and that] He would punish me? Why did He not leave me be? And once He created me, I obey Him — He is my Lord; why does He command me to prostrate to one other than Him, namely Ādam? And when I refused to prostrate to Ādam, why did He drive me off and curse me and make me damned, when I said nothing except that I worship none but my Lord alone, that I do not prostrate to any but Allah — and He drove me off, and He knows. Allah, when He knew in His pre-eternity that if He commanded me to prostrate to Ādam I would not prostrate to him, why did He command me to prostrate to him? And when He cursed me and drove me off and made me damned, me and everyone who followed me, why did He leave me in this world and give me power over the children of Ādam, [so that] I lead them astray and seduce them? And I asked that He defer me to the end of time, and He accepted this from me too. And He knows that a world with no evil in it is better than a world with evil in it. Why did He not relieve people of me and kill me? [15]

, Blessed and Exalted, answered: the answer to all these specious arguments is simply that his first statement is not true in his own case. He said: I am his Creator and I am his Lord; if I am his Creator and his Lord, then I am not questioned about what I do. The Lord, the Creator, disposes as He wills. He first acknowledged that Allah is his Creator and his Lord and his Master. If this is true, there is nothing

nothing is incumbent upon him but to comply with everything He has commanded him, nothing more. So his saying that he is a servant of Allah — this is not true in his own view, and for this reason he raises these objections. This specious argument of Iblīs is the one that has led the sects astray from the beginning of time to the end of time. He said that he was better than Adam: this one was created from clay, while he was created from light. He had worshipped Allah for so many thousands of years, brought near to Allah, while this one was created today from clay — how can he be better than me? He did not know that Allah does whatever He wills. So when the first of the prophets, Nūḥ, upon him be blessing and peace, came, his people said:

(Q. 2:54). Allah, Blessed and Exalted, recounts in this āya the story of the Children of Israel with Firʿawn. The Firʿawn of Mūsā was named Muṣʿab b. al-Rayyān, or al-Walīd b. Muṣʿab. [32] He was king of Egypt for four hundred years, [33] he never once suffered pain in his head, no illness ever befell him, every day he would eat a camel, and he would not go to the privy except once in forty days. After that,
took hold of him. He said that he was a god and not a servant, and so he laid claim to lordship:
I know of no god for you other than me
(Q. 28:38). After that he claimed beyond that:
I am your lord, the most high

(Q. 79:24). This Firʿawn saw a dream in which a fire came out of the dwellings of the Children of Israel and burned his dwellings and his kingdoms, all of them. The soothsayers said to him: a child will be born among the Children of Israel, and in him will lie the passing of your kingship, [34] this is the meaning of your dream. He said: the Children of Israel are my slaves; it is not possible that a child be born among them who takes away my kingship. So then: everyone born among the Children of Israel who is male, I must kill him. So he killed, from among the boys then present, twenty thousand boys, and every male child born among the Children of Israel he would kill, until he had killed ninety thousand children[35] along with the twenty thousand — this is one hundred thousand and ten thousand, all of this in pursuit of Mūsā alone. And the tongue of divinity was addressing him: the child whose killing you seek, you will rear him in your house and on your lap, and you will spend on him, until he becomes the cause of your destruction at his hands, in spite of you. So Mūsā was born, as will come in [Sūrat] al-Qaṣaṣ, and the cause of the destruction

of Firʿawn was Mūsā, upon him be blessing and peace. When Allah destroyed Firʿawn and his people, Mūsā asked Allah to give him a book by which to guide his people, the Children of Israel, in which there would be the lawful and the forbidden, the command and the prohibition. So Allah commanded him to fast forty nights. [36] Forty nights, not like our fasting: its nights and its days [alike], not at all. This is eighty nights. He did not break his fast for the space of forty days, night and day, and he felt no hunger, because he was turned toward the Presence. In a single day
he went to al-Khiḍr for half a day. He said:
Bring us our midday meal; we have met with hardship from this journey of ours

He went to a created being: he grew hungry in half a day. But when he turned toward the Real he remained eighty days, that is, forty days together with their nights, and he felt no hunger. For this reason the Messenger ﷺ said:
“Whoever is sincere toward Allah for forty days, wisdom wells up from his heart and runs upon his tongue.”
[37] This is the basis of the
seven nights and eight days in succession

And when you said: Mūsā, we will not believe you until we see Allah plainly, so the thunderbolt seized you while you were looking on. Then We raised you up after your death, so that you might be thankful. And We cast shade over you
(Q. 2:57): We covered you with the cloud.
and We sent down upon you the manna and the quails
Eat of the good things We have provided you
: and do not hoard. But they were ungrateful for the favour and they hoarded, so it was cut off from them.
And they did not wrong Us, but they were wronging themselves
(Q. 2:57): because its evil consequence falls upon them.
And when We said: Enter this town
and eat from it wherever you wish, freely
: amply, with no restriction in it.
is that which removes sins, and it is
your sins will be forgiven you, and We shall increase the doers of good. Then those who did wrong substituted
a word other than the one that had been said to them
, and they entered crawling on their backsides. They were commanded to prostrate and to say
, but they did not prostrate; rather they entered crawling on their backsides and said
We sent down upon those who did wrong a plague
from the heaven, because they were transgressing
(Q. 2:59): on account of their transgression, their going outside obedience. When they were in the trackless waste they said:

O Mūsā, where are we to get what we may eat? So tables of food came down upon them from heaven and they ate; and whenever the time of the midday meal came, the food would come down in the finest state it could be, and they would eat, and the table would be taken up until the time of its setting out on the morrow.

They said: Where are we to get clothing? Allah, Blessed and Exalted, guaranteed that their garments would neither be soiled nor wear out. Then they said: Where are we to get what we may drink? So he [Mūsā] struck the rock, and twelve springs gushed forth from it. Then they said: The sun is harming us,

So Allah brought clouds that screened them, so that they did not feel the heat of the sun. Then they complained of the darkness at night, so Allah set up pillars of light in the desert of the wilderness, all of it. All of this was through the blessing of Mūsā, who was with them. These are the merits of companionship. They, along with their ruin, their contravention of Allah's command, and the punishment's befalling them, had Mūsā and Hārūn among them, and they were given these kinds of blessing, all of it, because of Mūsā and Hārūn. Hārūn and Mūsā are among Allah's righteous servants, yet when the two of them kept company with these transgressors and remained with them forty years in the wilderness, they too tasted of the punishment because of the companionship, just as the transgressors found the blessing because of the companionship. All good is in companionship and all evil is in companionship.
O Allah, bless our master Muḥammad and grant [him] peace.
